The visarga of सः is dropped before a consonant.
पुनः is पुनर्: its visarga stands for r, which reappears before a vowel.

samasa.literal: struck by the stroke of the palm
samasa.sense: felled by the blow of her open hand

samasa.literal: on the surface of the earth

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (राजन् becomes राज at the end of a tatpuruṣa)

morph.note: Perfect of नि + √पत्: reduplicated प-पात with vṛddhi in the third singular.
Past participle of उद् + √स्था: the s of स्था is lost after उद् and d becomes t (उद् + स्थित → उत्थित). Active in sense: ‘having risen’.

mantras.anvaya: तलप्रहाराभिहतः (सः) महीतले निपपात। सः दैत्यराजः सहसा पुनः एव तथा उत्थितः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the first has the understood subject Śumbha (qualified by तलप्रहाराभिहतः) with निपपात; the second has सः दैत्यराजः with the participle उत्थितः as predicate.
mantras.lit: Struck by the blow of her palm, (he) fell down on the surface of the earth. That king of the Daityas at once rose up again, just so.
mantras.tr: Felled by the blow of her open hand, he crashed to the ground — and at once the Daitya king was on his feet again.
mantras.tr_note: तथा, ‘just so (as before)’, is absorbed into ‘on his feet again’.

comm.t: The open-handed blow of 10.20 knocks Śumbha to the ground, but he rises at once. The fight is not yet over.
A modern reading: the narrative repeatedly lets Śumbha rise. His strength is real; what defeats him is not weakness but the One he fights.

sandhi.note: a + u → o (प्रगृह्योच्चैः); visarga after ai before the voiced d is sounded as r (उच्चैर्देवीं).
Final m before a consonant is anusvāra (देवीं गगनम्); before a vowel it simply joins it (गगनमास्थितः).

samasa.sense: fighting in mid-air, with nothing beneath her feet

morph.note: आ + √स्था ‘to mount, go to’ with an object (गगनम्); the past participle is active in sense: ‘(he) had gone up into the sky’.
Perfect middle of √युध्: reduplicated यु-युध्-ए. With the instrumental तेन, ‘fought with him’.
Absolutive of प्र + √ग्रह्, with samprasāraṇa of the root (ग्रह् → गृह्) before ल्यप्.

mantras.anvaya: (सः) उत्पत्य च देवीं प्रगृह्य उच्चैः गगनम् आस्थितः। तत्र अपि सा चण्डिका निराधारा तेन युयुधे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: Śumbha (understood subject) with two absolutives (उत्पत्य, प्रगृह्य) and the participle आस्थितः; then the Goddess with युयुधे and the instrumental तेन.
mantras.lit: And having leapt up and seized the Goddess, (he) went up high into the sky. Even there Caṇḍikā, without support, fought with him.
mantras.tr: He sprang up, seized the Goddess, and rose high into the sky; and there too, with nothing to stand on, Caṇḍikā fought him.

comm.t: Śumbha carries the fight into the air. The Goddess needs no ground under her: निराधारा, ‘without a support’, she fights on in the sky.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same word as a name, निराधारा (132), where it means ‘she who depends on nothing’ — a metaphysical attribute. Here the word is literal: she fights in mid-air. The two senses meet, but the texts are separate.
A modern reading: Śumbha moves the battle off the earth, as if a change of ground could change its outcome. The Goddess, who rests on nothing, is not moved by it.

words.g: n. acc. sg.; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies नियुद्धम्

sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant is anusvāra; likewise प्रथमं सिद्ध-.

samasa.vigraha: सिद्धाः च मुनयः च सिद्धमुनयः; सिद्धमुनीनां विस्मयः सिद्धमुनिविस्मयः; तस्य कारकम्
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (कारक, an agent noun, governs its object in the genitive), containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (सिद्धमुनिविस्मय) and an itaretara dvandva (सिद्धमुनि)
samasa.literal: maker of the wonder of siddhas and sages
samasa.sense: a fight that astonished the siddhas and the sages
samasa.alt: सिद्धमुनि may also be a karmadhāraya, ‘perfected sages’ (सिद्धाः मुनयः); the dvandva, two classes of onlookers, fits the Epic idiom better.

morph.note: Perfect of √कृ, third person dual: reduplicated च-क्र-अतुः. The dual verb takes the two subjects joined by च (दैत्यः चण्डिका च).
Taken as an adjective of नियुद्धम्: ‘a first (fight)’, i.e. one never seen before. It could also be adverbial, ‘first’, but no second fight follows, so the first sense fits.

mantras.anvaya: तदा दैत्यः चण्डिका च खे परस्परं प्रथमं सिद्धमुनिविस्मयकारकं नियुद्धं चक्रतुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two subjects joined by च with a dual verb (चक्रतुः); the object नियुद्धम् carries two qualifiers (प्रथमम्, सिद्धमुनिविस्मयकारकम्).
mantras.lit: Then the Daitya and Caṇḍikā waged with each other in the sky a close fight, the first (of its kind), causing wonder to the siddhas and sages.
mantras.tr: There in the sky the Daitya and Caṇḍikā grappled with each other, a fight such as had never been seen, which filled the siddhas and the sages with wonder.
mantras.tr_note: प्रथमम्, ‘first (of its kind)’, is rendered ‘such as had never been seen’.

comm.t: The duel becomes a wrestling match (नियुद्ध, close combat without weapons) in the open sky, watched by the siddhas and sages.
A modern reading: at the end, all instruments are gone; the struggle is body to body. The text leaves nothing between the demon and the Goddess.

morph.note: Absolutive of the causative of उद् + √पत्: the causative suffix (-अय-) is dropped before -य: उद् + पात् + य. ‘Having made (him) fly up’, i.e. lifting him bodily.
Periphrastic perfect of the causative of √भ्रम् ‘to whirl’: भ्रामय + आम् + आस. ‘Made (him) whirl’, i.e. swung him round.
Perfect of √क्षिप्: reduplicated चि-क्षेप (the guttural of the reduplicated syllable becomes a palatal).

mantras.anvaya: ततः अम्बिका तेन सह सुचिरं नियुद्धं कृत्वा (तम्) उत्पात्य भ्रामयामास, (च) धरणीतले चिक्षेप।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive phrase (नियुद्धं … कृत्वा तेन सह), a second absolutive (उत्पात्य), and two finite verbs (भ्रामयामास, चिक्षेप) sharing the understood object ‘him’.
mantras.lit: Then Ambikā, having waged close combat with him for a very long time, lifted (him) up, whirled (him) round, and hurled (him) on the surface of the earth.
mantras.tr: After wrestling with him a long while, Ambikā lifted him high, whirled him round and flung him down to the earth.

comm.t: The Goddess ends the sky-fight: three verbs in sequence — lifting, whirling, hurling — bring Śumbha back to earth. The object (him) is understood throughout.
A modern reading: Śumbha had carried the Goddess into the sky (10.22); now she carries him and throws him down. The verse reverses his action exactly.

words.en: with the desire to kill Caṇḍikā
words.g: f. instr. sg.; compound (see Samāsa); instrumental of motive

samasa.vigraha: चण्डिकायाः निधनम् चण्डिकानिधनम्; तस्य इच्छा, तया
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (चण्डिकानिधन)
samasa.literal: by the wish for the death of Caṇḍikā

morph.note: Imperfect of अभि + √धाव् in the middle voice (ending -त); in 10.16 and 10.19 the same verb is active (अभ्यधावत्). √धाव् is ubhayapada, and the Epic uses both.
Absolutive of प्र + √आप् ‘to reach’: ‘having reached (the ground)’ — he lands and comes straight back at her.
An adjective in -इत from the noun वेग, ‘one in whom speed has arisen’: rushing, impetuous.

mantras.anvaya: क्षिप्तः सः धरणीं प्राप्य वेगितः मुष्टिम् उद्यम्य दुष्टात्मा चण्डिकानिधनेच्छया अभ्यधावत।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सः (with क्षिप्तः, वेगितः, दुष्टात्मा), two absolutive phrases (धरणीं प्राप्य; मुष्टिम् उद्यम्य), an instrumental of motive, and the verb अभ्यधावत.
mantras.lit: He, thrown, having reached the earth, raising his fist, impetuous — the wicked-souled one rushed forward with the desire to kill Caṇḍikā.
mantras.tr: Hurled down, he struck the earth, then sprang at her, fist raised, the evil one, still longing to kill Caṇḍikā.

comm.t: Thrown to the ground, Śumbha attacks once more with his fist. The verse repeats the language of 10.19 (मुष्टिमुद्यम्य) and of 10.18 (the wish to kill her): his intent never changes.
A modern reading: the narrative gives the demon the same gesture three times — raising his fist. Persistence without insight is the shape of his whole story.
